atoms.text: One way of examining societies is through class models. A class is described by factors such as education and occupation, wealth and income, and an association to a certain social and cultural group.

hint.text: The concept of class is widely used in English-speaking countries. In Germany, concepts such as Schicht and Milieu are more commonly used.
hint.label: Info

atoms.text: Many societies can be broadly divided into a small upper class, a large middle class as well as a large lower class.
atoms.sound: Many societies can be broadly divided into a small upper class, a large middle class as well as a large lower class.

atoms.text: In addition, the term working class can be classified as somewhere between the middle and lower classes.
atoms.sound: In addition, the term working class can be classified as somewhere between the middle and lower classes.

atoms.text: Since the middle class comprises groups that are sometimes very different, it is often further differentiated into the higher and lower middle classes.
atoms.sound: Since the middle class comprises groups that are sometimes very different, it is often further differentiated into the higher and lower middle classes.

atoms.text: Despite all the differences within one class, fundamental similarities can be outlined that many individuals in the respective classes share.

atoms.a: Work is often physical, often manual or service jobs with little financial security.
Income is usually stable and based on good education and a regular paid job.
Most money comes from family wealth, not from having a job.
The term blue-collar jobs is derived from the typical work clothes worn by mechanics and other tradesmen.

end.text: Other terms such as white-collar jobs for office workers and pink-collar jobs for professions in the social sector have derived from this.

atoms.a: Very unstable and low income. People often face poor living and working conditions.

atoms.text: Not only the middle class, but also the working class is often further subdivided. In the UK, for example, a distinction is often made between a skilled working class and an unskilled working class …
atoms.sound: Not only the middle class, but also the working class is often further subdivided. In the UK, for example, a distinction is often made between a skilled working class and an unskilled working class …

atoms.text: … whereas, with regard to the USA, sociologist Dennis Gilbert contrasted the working class with the working poor.
atoms.sound: … whereas, with regard to the USA, sociologist Dennis Gilbert contrasted the working class with the working poor.

atoms.text: So, the working poor, who can barely make a living from their work, can be classified as the lower class.
atoms.sound: So, the working poor, who can barely make a living from their work, can be classified as the lower class.

atoms.text: Class models such as Gilbert's are therefore always heavily dependent on the society under investigation and its historical circumstances. They cannot be readily transferred to other countries and times. However, public and class consciousness often differs from empirical studies.

hint.label: Vocabulary

atoms.b: In modern societies, the idea of social mobility plays an important role. During the second half of the 20th century, especially in the post World War II decades, there has been a great economic ((++upturn downfall)), combined with strong growth in prosperity. Many people in the middle class experienced that hard work could lead to ((++upward sideways)) mobility.

This idea has been firmly established ever since, although social ((++inequality equality)) has increased significantly in recent years. New research shows that the underlying concept of ((++meritocracy capitalism)) does not adequately describe social reality, but still, it continues to convince many people. This seems paradoxical when you consider that at the same time many people in the middle class now fear ((++downwards upwards)) mobility rather than moving up in the social hierarchy.

The fear of decline does not stop at class boundaries. In many countries, the once broad and self-assured ((++working_class upper_class)), which derived its identity from its work and social cohesion, has vanished. Instead, a precarious class is growing, characterised by ((++insecurity prosperity)) and the loss of social ties.
